article.title: Why Productivity Is Harder to Measure in a Digital Business
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Productivity sounds simple: compare output with the resources used to produce it. In a factory, analysts can count units, labor hours, machines, and materials. Digital businesses make this calculation harder because some of their most valuable inputs and outputs are intangible. Software, data, algorithms, organizational knowledge, and improved workflows can create value without appearing like a new physical machine.

Consider a bank that builds an internal tool to automate document review. Employees may process applications faster, make fewer errors, and spend more time on complex cases. The improvement is real, but measuring the output is difficult. The number of applications may stay unchanged while quality and speed improve. If the productivity metric only counts completed applications, part of the gain disappears from the measurement.

Digital products create another problem: marginal cost can be very low. Once software is built, an additional user may cost little to serve. A company can therefore increase the number of users dramatically without a proportional increase in employees or physical capital. This looks like high productivity, but analysts still need to decide how to value free services, bundled features, or quality improvements.

Investment measurement is difficult as well. Traditional accounting distinguishes expenses from assets, but economically valuable capabilities do not always fit neatly into that boundary. Employee training, process redesign, data cleaning, experimentation, and management effort can create organizational capital. Some of this spending is recorded as a current expense even when the benefit lasts for years. If analysts treat all of it as consumption rather than investment, they may misunderstand how much productive capacity the company is building.

AI makes the issue more visible. A firm may buy an AI tool but gain little because workflows, incentives, data access, and employee skills are unchanged. Another firm may spend heavily on redesigning processes before seeing measurable output. During the transition, costs rise first and productivity appears weak. Later, once the organization adapts, the same technology may generate larger gains. This timing gap can make early measurements misleading.

Quality adjustment is another challenge. Suppose a customer-support team handles the same number of cases with the same number of employees, but response time falls from twelve hours to two hours and customer satisfaction rises. Has productivity increased? Economically, probably yes. A narrow quantity metric may say no. Digital transformation often changes speed, reliability, personalization, and convenience before it changes the number of units produced.

This does not mean productivity statistics are useless. It means managers should avoid relying on one measure. A digital business can combine traditional metrics such as revenue per employee with operational measures such as cycle time, error rates, automation coverage, customer outcomes, and capacity released for higher-value work. No single metric captures everything.

Managers should also distinguish local productivity from company-wide productivity. Automating one team can make that team faster while moving work to another department. For example, a self-service system may reduce call-center work but increase engineering maintenance. Measuring only the first team exaggerates the total gain. End-to-end process measurement is therefore important.

The broader lesson is that digital productivity is partly a measurement problem and partly an organizational problem. Technology can create value through assets that are hard to see, quality changes that are hard to count, and process redesign that takes time. When a dashboard shows little improvement, managers should not immediately conclude that the technology failed. They should ask whether the right output, quality, investment, and system boundaries are being measured.
paragraphs.zh: 數位企業的 productivity 比工廠難衡量，因為 software、data、algorithm、流程與 organizational knowledge 等無形資產不容易被傳統投入產出指標捕捉。自動化可能讓速度與品質改善，但處理件數不變；免費服務、bundled feature 與低 marginal cost 也讓 output 價值難估。Training、process redesign、data cleaning 等支出可能創造多年價值，會計上卻常被當期費用處理。AI 導入還有 timing gap：成本與流程改造先發生，產出改善後出現。管理者應搭配 revenue per employee、cycle time、error rate、automation coverage、customer outcome 等多種指標，並從 end-to-end process 看是否只是把工作移到其他部門。
paragraphs.ja: デジタル企業のproductivityは、software、data、algorithm、workflow、organizational knowledgeなど無形のinputとoutputが多いため測定が難しくなります。自動化でspeedやqualityが改善しても処理件数が同じなら、数量指標では効果が見えません。training、process redesign、data cleaningなどは長期的能力を作っても会計上は当期費用になる場合があります。AI導入では費用と組織変更が先に発生し、成果が後から出るtiming gapもあります。管理者はrevenue per employeeだけでなくcycle time、error rate、automation coverage、customer outcomeなどを組み合わせ、end-to-endで仕事が別部門へ移っただけではないかも確認する必要があります。

quiz.question: Why can digital productivity gains be hard to see?
quiz.answer: Because quality, intangible investment, and process improvements may not appear in simple quantity metrics.

quiz.question: Why is end-to-end measurement useful?
quiz.answer: It shows whether work was eliminated or merely shifted elsewhere.

quiz.question: Output: Name one productivity metric besides revenue per employee.
